Heading: Govt Calls All-Party Meeting On July 19 Ahead Of Monsoon Session; Opposition Set To Raise Key Issues
Summary:
• Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced the Monsoon Session of Parliament from July 20 to August 13, 2026.
• The Centre has convened an all-party meeting on July 19 to discuss the legislative agenda.
• Opposition parties plan to challenge the government on issues like the NEET-UG paper leak and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh's remarks.
Content:
The Centre has convened an all-party meeting on July 19, a day before the commencement of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, during which the government is expected to outline its legislative agenda while opposition parties are likely to highlight the issues they intend to raise in both Houses.

The customary meeting, held before every Parliament session, will begin at 11 am, officials said.

Government to Outline Legislative Agenda

The government is expected to push an extensive legislative agenda during the session, with several key Bills likely to be introduced and taken up for discussion.

The Monsoon Session of Parliament will be held from July 20 to August 13, as announced earlier by Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju.

"On the recommendation of the Government of India, Hon'ble President Smt. Droupadi Murmu has approved the summoning of both the Houses of Parliament for the Monsoon Session 2026. The Session will commence on July 20, 2026 and continue till August 13, 2026, for meaningful debate, discussion and decisions on issues of national importance," Rijiju said in a post on X.

Opposition Likely to Raise Key Issues

The Opposition is expected to corner the government over several issues, including the NEET-UG paper leak case and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh's remarks on casualties during Operation Sindoor.

The Congress has already moved a breach of privilege notice against the Defence Minister over his comments.

Political Realignments Ahead of Session

The upcoming session is also expected to witness heated exchanges amid recent political realignments across several opposition parties.

The Trinamool Congress (TMC) has witnessed significant turmoil following its defeat in the Assembly elections. Twenty of its MPs have reportedly merged with the National Citizens Party of India and have sought separate seating arrangements in the Lok Sabha. Additionally, three TMC Rajya Sabha MPs resigned from the Upper House before joining the BJP.

Meanwhile, the Shiv Sena (UBT) has also suffered a setback, with six of its Lok Sabha MPs joining the Shiv Sena led by Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde. Earlier, seven AAP Rajya Sabha MPs had also joined the BJP.

JPC Report on Constitution Amendment Bill Expected

Ahead of the Monsoon Session, the Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) examining the proposed 130th Constitution Amendment Bill is expected to adopt its report on July 17 before submitting it to Parliament.

The proposed Bill has triggered political debate over a provision that seeks the automatic removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers, and Union or State ministers from office if they remain in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days in cases involving serious offences.

The report is expected to be one of the significant documents tabled during the session.

Heading: AP emerging as defence manufacturing hub: Rajnath Singh
Summary:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned the stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy in Visakhapatnam.
• Singh highlighted Andhra Pradesh as a growing hub for indigenous defence manufacturing, citing projects like the AMCA testing centre and BDL facilities.
• The warship, built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, strengthens India's maritime security and operational reach in the Indian Ocean Region.
Content:
VISAKHAPATNAM: The Indian Navy commissioned the indigenously built stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri into its Eastern Fleet in Visakhapatnam on Saturday, marking the induction of the sixth of the seven Project 17A Nilgiri-class stealth frigates.

At the commissioning ceremony, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh underscored India’s progress in indigenous defence production and described Andhra Pradesh as an emerging centre for defence and aerospace manufacturing.

“Andhra Pradesh has emerged as a new powerhouse of India’s defence and aerospace manufacturing. It is playing its role across air, water, land, and the unmanned domain,” he remarked, adding, “This means the weapon systems that we once used to import from abroad will now be produced near our own Vizag,” he said.

He cited the foundation stone laying for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) Core Integration and Flight Testing Centre at Puttaparthi and Bharat Dynamics Limited’s upcoming Naval Systems Manufacturing Facility in Anakapalli, where autonomous underwater vehicles, torpedoes and underwater countermeasure systems will be produced.

“AMCA in the skies, BDL’s naval systems in the depths of the ocean, Kurnool’s drones in the unmanned domain, and today, INS Mahendragiri on the surface of the sea signify that Andhra Pradesh is now contributing to India’s defence strength across every sphere,” he noted.

The Defence Minister also underlined the changing character of warfare, observing that technological advances were transforming military operations without diminishing the importance of conventional capabilities.

“Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military power,” he remarked. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, drones, cyber warfare, hypersonic weapons and space-based systems, he emphasised, complement rather than replace conventional military platforms.

Citing Operation Sindoor, the Defence Minister pointed to the operation as an illustration of the effective integration of modern technologies with conventional military capability.

The frigate was designed by the Indian Navy’s Warship Design Bureau and built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited, Mumbai. With over 75% indigenous content, the 6,670-tonne warship can attain 28 knots. It is configured for fleet air defence, anti-surface and anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction, surveillance and HADR.

It carries supersonic and medium-range missiles, stealth features, sensors, network-centric systems, anti-submarine weapons and a multi-role helicopter. It could also be equipped with the BrahMos missile system.

Describing maritime security as integral to India’s economic interests, the Defence Minister observed that secure sea lanes were essential for trade, energy security and resilient supply chains. He noted that the Indian Navy’s humanitarian assistance, anti-piracy operations and evacuation missions had reinforced its role as a first responder and a preferred security partner in the Indo-Pacific.

Referring to Operation Urja Suraksha during the West Asia conflict, he stated that the Navy had safely escorted 18 merchant vessels carrying cargo worth more than Rs 9,000 crore.

Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan described INS Mahendragiri as another milestone in indigenous warship construction that would strengthen the Navy’s operational capability.

Built with contributions from more than 200 Indian industries, including several MSMEs, the frigate is named after the Mahendragiri mountain range in the Eastern Ghats and will enhance the Navy’s operational reach in the Indian Ocean Region.

Heading: Hizbul Mujahideen steps up recruitment with more Pakistani fighters
Summary:
• Intelligence officials report that the terrorist organization Hizbul Mujahideen, led by Syed Salahuddin, is shifting strategy to recruit Pakistani fighters for operations in Jammu and Kashmir.
• The group aims to revive separatist sentiment and increase infiltration attempts from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.
• Indian security agencies are monitoring these renewed efforts to destabilize the region.
Content:
Intelligence officials say Hizbul Mujahideen has begun a fresh recruitment drive with a greater focus on Pakistani fighters, infiltration and reviving separatist sentiment in Jammu and Kashmir. Security agencies have cautioned that the outfit's renewed efforts should not be underestimatedCity & Local Guides

New Delhi: The Hizbul Mujahideen, once projected as a home-grown terror outfit in Jammu and Kashmir, has recently begun changing its strategy.

The group, which had remained largely inactive after Indian security forces dismantled most of its networks in Jammu and Kashmir, has now launched a fresh recruitment drive.History

An Intelligence Bureau official said that the recruitment pattern is, however, different and today the Hizbul Mujahideen has more Pakistani fighters as compared to the local Kashmiris.

“This clearly shows that the local Kashmiris no longer want to be part of this outfit; hence a decision to recruit Pakistanis in large numbers has been taken,” the official said.

The official said that on July 8, a meeting was held to commemorate the death anniversary of slain Hizbul Mujahideen commander Burhan Wani.

The members of the outfit, which is headquartered in Muzaffarabad in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), discussed a range of issues that involved recruitment and strategy. The Hizbul Mujahideen has been under immense pressure from the Pakistani establishment to regroup and commence operations in Jammu and Kashmir.

Post Operation Sindoor, the Hizbul Mujahideen has remained relatively quiet and not focused on its future operations. With the Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) down owing to its top leaders missing in action, the emphasis to commence operations in Jammu and Kashmir largely falls on the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and Hizbul Mujahideen.

“The Pakistani establishment is engaging the Lashkar-e-Taiba in the various trouble-torn regions in Pakistan. The terror group has been tasked with taking on outfits such as the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP),” another official said.

With the Lashkar engaged in Pakistan, its spy agency, Inter Services Intelligence, wants to push the Hizbul Mujahideen and is expecting it to restart operations in Jammu and Kashmir.

The outfit, which has struggled to gain traction in Jammu and Kashmir in recent years, is now looking to recruit Pakistani nationals into its ranks. In addition to this, the ISI has also instructed the Hizbul Mujahideen to be ready for infiltrations.

Nearly 100 Hizbul Mujahideen terrorists are reportedly waiting at launch pads in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir to infiltrate Jammu and Kashmir. At the same time, the outfit’s top leadership has been directed to intensify its propaganda campaign in the Valley.

The outfit’s top leadership, led by Syed Salahuddin, has been directed to step up efforts to recruit youth in Kashmir. Even as it plans to induct large numbers of Pakistani nationals, the group is also expected to strengthen its local presence by bringing more Kashmiris into its ranks.City & Local Guides

Another official said that these moves being made by the Hizbul Mujahideen cannot be taken lightly. The focus would not just be on recruiting terrorists and attempting attacks in Jammu and Kashmir.

The Hizbul Mujahideen has a history of driving a separatist narrative. It would scout for persons in Jammu and Kashmir who can re-introduce separatism in the Union Territory. In fact, this move would be more dangerous when compared to actual terror strikes.

One of the key drivers of terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir has been separatism. Separatist leaders have long been accused of radicalising young people, encouraging stone-pelting and persuading them to join terror groups to fight the Indian security forces.

Officials say Hizbul Mujahideen’s revival plan rests on two key elements: recruiting more terrorists from Pakistan and reviving separatist sentiment in the Valley.

While the outfit’s comeback may not be easy given the heavy losses it has suffered at the hands of Indian security agencies since 2016, officials caution that the renewed push to revive militant operations in Jammu and Kashmir cannot be taken lightly.History

Heading: Future wars may use AI, but trained soldiers will win them: Rajnath Singh
Summary:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned INS Mahendragiri in Visakhapatnam, highlighting India's indigenous defence manufacturing capabilities.
• Singh emphasized that while AI is transforming warfare, national resolve and trained soldiers remain essential for victory.
• He reaffirmed India's commitment to the SAGAR vision, positioning the Indian Navy as a net security provider in the Indo-Pacific region.
Content:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said future wars may involve Artificial Intelligence but will ultimately be won by trained soldiers and national resolve. Commissioning INS Mahendragiri, he stressed balancing advanced technologies with conventional military strength and highlighted India's growing defence manufacturing capabilitiesWorld news coverage

Visakhapatnam: Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and robust military power, Defence Minister Rajanth Singh said on Saturday.

Speaking at the commissioning ceremony of INS Mahendragiri here, Singh also said Andhra Pradesh has emerged as a new powerhouse of India’s defence and aerospace manufacturing.Geographic Reference

Highlighting the government’s balanced approach towards defence modernisation, Singh said India is investing in next-generation technologies while simultaneously strengthening conventional military capabilities.

He cited Operation Sindoor as an example of the effective integration of conventional and modern capabilities to safeguard national security.

“Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and the capable military power. So, I would say that new technologies and conventional platforms are not opposed to each other, but supplement each other, complete each other. Without conventional platforms, new technologies are incomplete in themselves,” he said.

According to Singh, it is certain that new technologies have reshaped warfare, but they have not diminished the role of conventional warfare means.South Asians & Diaspora

The strong conventional capability that is still necessary for the fulfilment of basic principles of war is as important as it was before. Emphasising that maritime security and economic security are closely interconnected, Singh said the seas remain vital for trade, supply chains, energy security and economic growth.

He reaffirmed the government’s commitment to the Security and Growth for All in the Region (SAGAR) vision in the Indo-Pacific. Calling India a net security provider and trusted regional partner, Singh said the Indian Navy has consistently demonstrated its commitment through humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations, anti-piracy missions and the evacuation of Indian and foreign nationals from conflict-hit regions, earning recognition as both a first responder and a preferred security partner.

Referring to the Indian Navy’s role during the recent West Asia conflict, Singh said under Operation Urja Suraksha, the Navy safely escorted 18 merchant vessels carrying essential cargo valued at more than Rs 9,000 crore, highlighting its role in protecting not only national security but also India’s economic interests.

The defence minister said the successful induction of the warship demonstrates India’s growing capability to design, build and deploy complex frontline combat platforms through indigenous expertise.

The warship is equipped with an indigenous rocket launcher, torpedo launchers, an Integrated Anti-Submarine Defence System, an Electronic Warfare suite and a Close-In Weapon System, making it a formidable and resilient combat platform capable of operating in challenging maritime environments.World news coverage

Describing INS Mahendragiri as a “blue-water warship”, Singh said it can effectively counter threats from the air, enemy vessels on the surface and submarines hidden beneath the sea, and can protect India’s maritime interests not only near the coastline but also in distant and deep oceans during prolonged deployments.

The union minister said the commissioning of Mahendragiri comes at a time when the nature of warfare is rapidly evolving with the emergence of drones, artificial intelligence, cyber warfare, hypersonic weapons, space-based capabilities and unmanned systems.

However, he stressed that conventional military capabilities continue to remain the bedrock of effective national defence. The Union Minister described INS Mahendragiri as a symbol of the nation’s commitment to building a technologically advanced and combat-ready Navy capable of meeting future security challenges while protecting India’s maritime interests.

He expressed confidence that INS Mahendragiri would further strengthen India’s maritime strategy by enhancing the security of the eastern seaboard, extending the country’s blue-water operational reach and reinforcing its presence across the Indian Ocean Region.

Singh said indigenous warship construction goes beyond building combat platforms as it strengthens design capability, technological expertise, skilled manpower and the broader maritime industrial ecosystem.

He noted that shipbuilding supports sectors including steel, electronics, sensors, propulsion systems, software, precision engineering and logistics while generating employment and fostering innovation.

Reiterating the government’s vision to establish India as a global hub for shipbuilding and maritime defence innovation, the Union Minister said initiatives such as Maritime India Vision 2030, the Maritime Development Fund, the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Scheme and the Shipbuilding Development Scheme are aimed at modernising ports, expanding inland waterways, strengthening logistics networks, enhancing industrial capacity and boosting self-reliance.

He also called upon young entrepreneurs, engineers, innovators, researchers and investors to contribute to nation-building by developing advanced technologies and defence systems that would shape future warfare and strengthen India’s self-reliance in the defence sector.

Singh said the induction of Mahendragiri marks another milestone in India’s journey towards defence self-reliance and strengthens the Navy’s operational capability in safeguarding the country’s maritime interests across the Indian Ocean Region and beyond.South Asians & Diaspora

However, he stressed that conventional military capabilities continue to remain the bedrock of effective national defence.
The Union Minister described INS Mahendragiri as a symbol of the nation's commitment to building a technologically advanced and combat-ready Navy capable of meeting future security challenges while protecting India's maritime interests.
He expressed confidence that INS Mahendragiri would further strengthen India's maritime strategy by enhancing the security of the eastern seaboard, extending the country's blue-water operational reach and reinforcing its presence across the Indian Ocean Region.
Singh said indigenous warship construction goes beyond building combat platforms as it strengthens design capability, technological expertise, skilled manpower and the broader maritime industrial ecosystem.
He noted that shipbuilding supports sectors including steel, electronics, sensors, propulsion systems, software, precision engineering and logistics while generating employment and fostering innovation.
Reiterating the government's vision to establish India as a global hub for shipbuilding and maritime defence innovation, the Union Minister said initiatives such as Maritime India Vision 2030, the Maritime Development Fund, the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Scheme and the Shipbuilding Development Scheme are aimed at modernising ports, expanding inland waterways, strengthening logistics networks, enhancing industrial capacity and boosting self-reliance.
He also called upon young entrepreneurs, engineers, innovators, researchers and investors to contribute to nation-building by developing advanced technologies and defence systems that would shape future warfare and strengthen India's self-reliance in the defence sector.
Singh said the induction of Mahendragiri marks another milestone in India's journey towards defence self-reliance and strengthens the Navy's operational capability in safeguarding the country's maritime interests across the Indian Ocean Region and beyond.

Summary:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Indonesia visit secured major BrahMos and Astra missile export deals, marking a significant defence breakthrough.
• The Indian Navy commissioned the indigenously built INS Mahendragiri, highlighting India's growing self-reliance in warship manufacturing.
• The Indian Army and Air Force are seeking to increase Agniveer retention caps based on operational data and training requirements.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Indonesia visit delivers India’s biggest Southeast Asia defence export breakthrough with BrahMos and Astra deals as the Agnipath scheme heads for an overhaul and China’s new submarine missile shifts the Indo-Pacific balance. Firstpost tracks the week’s top defence developments.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Jakarta has produced India’s biggest defence export win in Southeast Asia so far. Indonesia is now the third country, after the Philippines and Vietnam, to operate the BrahMos cruise missile. This time it comes paired with Astra, India’s beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile, an entirely different weapons category being sold alongside it.
What’s actually being sold : BrahMos is a known quantity by now. Built jointly with Russia, its reputation only grew stronger after India used it operationally during Operation Sindoor last year. A missile that’s been fired in combat sells itself in a way no defence expo ever could. Astra is the newer piece of this story. It’s a DRDO-built missile with long strike range and speeds well past Mach 4, and Bharat Dynamics will now integrate it onto Indonesia’s Su-30 fighter fleet alongside a local Indonesian firm. That last part matters more than it sounds, integration work isn’t a one-time sale, it locks India into servicing and upgrading Jakarta’s frontline fighter squadron for years to come.
Why Jakarta is actually buying this : Indonesia is hedging. Its military has traditionally bought from Russia, the US and Europe all at once, and that mix comes with real risk, sanctions exposure, spare parts getting political, being forced to pick a side. Buying from India lets Jakarta diversify without stepping directly into the middle of a US-China standoff it has no interest in joining. For an archipelagic country sitting right along some of the world’s busiest and most contested shipping lanes, staying unaligned isn’t idealism, it’s strategy.
The bigger pattern : Since Operation Sindoor, every BrahMos deal, the Philippines, Vietnam, now Indonesia, has moved faster and gone bigger than the one before it. Several more countries, including the UAE, are reportedly in talks. This is what India’s defence self-reliance push was always supposed to lead to eventually, not just building weapons for its own military, but actually taking market share in a region Russia and Western suppliers have dominated for decades.
The part that matters more than the missiles : Buried in this visit is a quieter decision to revive joint development of Sabang Port in Indonesia. Sabang sits right at the western mouth of the Strait of Malacca, close enough to India’s own upcoming transhipment hub at Great Nicobar that the two sit on opposite sides of the same chokepoint. This project was first floated back in 2018 and went nowhere. It’s back on the table now.
Malacca isn’t just any shipping lane, close to 80 per cent of China’s energy imports pass through it, a dependency Chinese strategists have openly worried about for years, they even have a name for it, the “Malacca dilemma.” An Indian-linked port at Sabang, sitting alongside Great Nicobar, gives India a presence on both sides of that chokepoint’s northern approach. Chinese analysts have already noticed, and they’re not reading it as a coincidence.
Great Nicobar is still years from being fully operational. Sabang isn’t meant to compete with it directly, it’s positioned more as a logistics and marine-services hub. But for the Indian Navy, that’s still useful, a forward base for anti-piracy patrols, disaster relief operations, and simply keeping an eye on Chinese naval movement into the eastern Indian Ocean. And unlike India’s other stalled port ambitions, Chabahar in Iran, Mongla in Bangladesh, this one has an advantage those didn’t, Indonesia actually wants it built too. That mutual interest is what gives it a real chance of surviving this time.
Why it matters : A long list of agreements came out of this visit, but two will outlast the joint statement. One is India establishing itself as a real defence exporter in a region Russia and the West have owned for decades. The other is a maritime foothold that quietly narrows China’s options at one of the most sensitive chokepoints on the map. Modi called it a “golden new chapter.” The missile deals are the part everyone will read about. Sabang, if it actually gets built this time, is the part that could genuinely change how this region looks a decade from now.
The advancement of drone warfare and lessons from the Russia-Ukraine and West Asia conflicts show how countries are quickly ramping up their UAV game. Three unrelated stories from this week point to the exact same conclusion that having the organisational agility to build, deploy, and adapt to new drone tactics at scale is crucial for all militaries.
Russia is now scaling a dedicated brigade, the 50th “Varyag” Unmanned Systems Brigade, to become a mainstay of its forces. It will report straight to the top of the military instead of a regional command. Russia had in 2024, it set up a unit called Rubicon to hunt down Ukrainian drone crews and jam their signals. It worked so well that Russian forces have also started flying strike drones that fly themselves along a set path, no radio signal needed, which makes them much harder to jam or shoot down. None of this is new technology. What changed is speed: Russia took something that worked on one battlefield and rolled it out across its entire army in months, not years. That’s usually the hardest thing for a big, slow-moving military to do.
Meanwhile, Nato and the US are chasing the same problem from the other direction, they’re behind, and trying to catch up. Nato countries have put together over $40 billion over five years just to detect and shoot down drones, not build them. They’ve also set up a shared marketplace, so any member country can buy tested counter-drone equipment quickly instead of running its own slow, separate tender process, plus a plan to train five times as many drone operators by 2027. Their reasoning: cheap drones, some costing just a few thousand dollars, have become a bigger daily problem than expensive missiles, and old-style air defence built for jet fighters and cruise missiles is too slow and too costly to use against them.
In the US, the Pentagon has gone even further. It has put one official in charge of nearly all American drone programmes across air, sea and land, ending years where the Army, Navy and Air Force each ran their own separate, disconnected drone efforts. The reason given: Russia is set to build over 7 million small drones this year, China controls most of the world’s drone parts, and the US has simply fallen behind on numbers.
What this means for India : Take away the details, and all three stories are saying the same thing: the problem isn’t the technology, it’s the organisation. India already has plenty of drone experience, from Pakistan’s incursions in the west to China’s activity near the LAC. But experience only helps if it gets turned into standard practice quickly. And that’s exactly where things get stuck, because India’s drone efforts are split across the Army, Navy, Air Force, DRDO and private industry, each moving at its own speed and answering to its own chain of command.
India’s counter-drone technology is already being built by DRDO and private firms, so that’s not really the weak point. The weak point is how fast India can buy and roll out that technology once it exists. A 32-country alliance just found a way to buy counter-drone gear fast by pooling all its members’ demand into one marketplace. The world’s richest military just decided that having four separate drone offices was slower than having one office in charge, even though each of those four offices had more money and expertise than most countries’ entire militaries. Russia, fighting under sanctions with far fewer resources than India, took one good drone unit and turned it into a nationwide model in under two years.
Why it matters : None of these are countries India should copy exactly. Russia’s expansion has come with its own problems around quality and training. Nato’s and the Pentagon’s fixes are only a few weeks old and still unproven. But all three are moving in the same direction, and that’s worth noticing. The real question for India isn’t whether it has good drones or good lessons from two active fronts, it clearly has both. The question is whether there’s a system in place to turn a frontline fix into force-wide practice before the next crisis hits, instead of it staying stuck inside one service’s silo.
China fired a submarine-launched ballistic missile into the South Pacific on July 6. It landed inside a nuclear-free zone that China itself signed up to. Australia, New Zealand and Japan all protested.
Here’s why it matters. Until now, Chinese submarines had to sail far out into the open Pacific to get America in range, which meant US and allied forces could track and hunt them the whole way. This missile changes that. Chinese submarines can now stay close to home, protected by China’s own navy and radar, and still hit distant targets. That’s a huge deal. It means China’s nuclear submarines are much harder to find and destroy than before.
What this means for India : The missile wasn’t aimed at India. But here’s the catch: once China’s submarines don’t need heavy escort to stay safe near home, its other attack submarines are freed up to go elsewhere. The Indian Ocean is the likely destination. China has also been sending “research” ships around the Indian Ocean for years, quietly mapping the seabed, which helps its submarines hide and helps them find India’s. India’s own underwater missile programme is still catching up. The answer isn’t building more missiles to match China one for one. It’s building better submarine-hunting capability and using India’s geographic advantage, since most Chinese ships still have to pass through narrow chokepoints India can watch closely.
On July 3, Xi Jinping promoted two officers to full general, the PLA’s highest active rank. Before this, the PLA, a force of over 2 million, had only four serving full generals. Years of purges had gutted the top ranks, and Xi is now rebuilding them on his own terms.
What it means for India : Officers who’ve watched two vice chairmen and a defence minister get purged in three years learn one lesson fast: don’t act without cover from the top. That should lower the odds of a local commander improvising at the LAC the way frontline units did before Galwan in 2020.
It cuts the other way too. When no one wants to make a call without Beijing’s sign-off, standoffs take longer to de-escalate, not less. India’s teams at the Special Representatives talks and the Western Theatre Command hotline should read future stalemates through that lens: not necessarily stonewalling, but a chain of command built to reward caution in both directions.
INS Mahendragiri will be commissioned at Visakhapatnam today, on July 11. It’s the sixth Project 17A frigate built at Mazagon Dock. Over 75 percent of the ship was built in India, and the design itself came from the Navy’s own Warship Design Bureau. It carries weapons for air, surface and submarine threats, along with electronic warfare systems and a combat management setup that connects everything together. Its engines let it run fast when needed but still cover long distances efficiently.
Why it matters : Getting six frigates like this into service in about a year gives the Navy more ships to actually patrol the Indian Ocean with. China’s navy has been growing steadily, so that extra presence matters. But the bigger story is the 75 percent figure. It shows India can now build a warship this complicated mostly on its own, instead of depending on foreign yards for the hard parts.
The Army has put out a tender for 450 Carl Gustaf Mark-IV launchers, to be manufactured in India along with spares and accessories. The new launcher has to weigh under 7 kg, last 1,500 rounds or 15 years, and hit targets 800 metres out. It also has to work in temperatures from -20°C to +50°C, so it can be used in Siachen just as easily as in the Rajasthan desert. The winning vendor gets 12 months to deliver, and countries sharing a land border with India can’t bid, which keeps China out.
Why it matters : infantry units have carried the Mark-III version of this launcher for years. It’s their main tool for taking out tanks and bunkers. A lighter launcher that lasts longer sounds like a small change, but for a soldier walking uphill with this on his back, weight makes a real difference. Small upgrades like this add up over time, even if they never make front-page news.
The first batch of Agniveers completes its four-year tenure later this year, and all three services want the exit door narrower than promised. The Army, Navy and Air Force have submitted proposals to the Department of Military Affairs seeking a sharp jump above the current 25 per cent retention cap as reported by Firstpost , the first real test of whether Agnipath survives contact with its own outcomes.
The numbers : The Navy is pushing hardest, seeking to retain up to 75 per cent of its Agniveers. The Army and Air Force are asking for around 50 per cent. Both would roughly double or triple the retention ceiling set when the scheme launched in 2022. A similar proposal was floated earlier and sent back for re-evaluation, so this isn’t the first attempt, and it may not clear easily this time either.
Why now : The pitch rests on four years of operational data the services didn’t have at launch. Agniveers have been present through Operation Sindoor and a stretch of high-tempo border deployment, and sources cite that experience as the trigger for the retention push. The underlying argument is about training economics as much as loyalty: the platforms India has inducted since Sindoor, more complex radars, precision-guided systems, integrated air defence, take longer to master than a four-year cycle allows for. Train someone for two years on a system and release them at year four, and the institutional knowledge walks out the door with them.
The fallback option : If the DMA doesn’t move the overall cap, the services have a workaround ready: skew retention by unit type rather than raise it across the board. The Army’s newly raised Bhairav battalions, light commando-style units built for hybrid warfare, are cited as the model, formations that could carry a much higher proportion of retained, experienced Agniveers while regular infantry continues to run closer to the original 75-25 release-retain split. That keeps the average retention number intact for the government’s messaging while giving specialised units the depth they’re asking for.
Why it matters : Agnipath was built on a specific trade: younger units, a lighter pension bill, a national talent pipeline into the civilian economy. Retention above 25 percent chips at all three, more experienced but older personnel, a bigger long-term salary and pension liability, and a smaller annual release cohort feeding the reservation quotas set up for the Coast Guard and defence PSUs. None of that makes the case for higher retention wrong. It just means the political framing of Agnipath as a lean, youth-first reform will need updating if the numbers land anywhere near what the Navy is asking for. The government has stayed publicly silent on both proposals. What it decides in the coming months will set the template not just for this batch, but for how Agnipath is recruited, trained and sold from here on.
Bengaluru’s radar establishment under DRDO has a new AESA radar family in the works, and one variant stands out: a Low Band Active Antenna Array built specifically to catch things that don’t want to be caught, low-observable aircraft, ships hugging the horizon, targets at long range. This isn’t a standalone project either. It’s meant to feed straight into Uttam, the radar slated for the Tejas Mk2.
On a separate track, DRDO has handed over two thermal management systems to BHEL for full-scale production, a pre-cooler heat exchanger and a condenser-heat exchanger. Both were originally built for the Tejas Mk1, but they’re being scaled up to deal with a much bigger problem: the AMCA runs hotter. Cramming AESA radar, electronic warfare gear and internal weapons bays into one airframe generates heat loads the older cooling systems were never designed for.
Why it matters : Nobody gets excited about a radar chip or a heat exchanger, but this is where fighter jets actually win or lose. A radar that overheats loses range. A jet that runs too hot glows brighter on infrared sensors, which defeats the entire point of stealth. So this is really about survivability, not electronics. And handing the cooling tech to BHEL instead of leaving it in a DRDO lab is the bigger tell here, it means India is trying to build actual manufacturing muscle for AMCA parts, not just prototypes that work once on a test bench.
The Navy has issued a Request for Information for a new sonar concept called CTLS, short for Containerised Theatre Level Sonar, and the idea behind it is simple. Instead of building a submarine-hunting sensor into a warship’s hull, you pack it into a standard container. Any ship with a certified A-frame and winch can carry it, frigates, OPVs, even support vessels that were never designed for anti-submarine work. Several units can link up and triangulate a submarine’s position across a wide area, switching between mono, bi and multi-static detection modes depending on the situation.
Why it matters : New warships take years to build, sometimes a decade from keel-laying to commissioning. CTLS skips that timeline though the system is still at the RFI stage, well short of a contract . The Navy can bolt sonar capability onto ships already in the water, which matters a lot given how active Chinese submarines have become in the Indian Ocean lately.
Adani Defence & Aerospace has begun construction on a ₹2,500 crore missile manufacturing complex in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh. What makes this one different from Adani’s other defence facilities is that it covers the full missile value chain, propellant production through to finished, mission-ready systems, all at one site. The company says it’ll build medium and long-range missiles here, create around 5,000 jobs, and pull in more than 50 MSMEs as suppliers. It joins Adani’s existing Gwalior plant, which already makes small arms for the forces.
You can read more about it here .
Why it matters : missile production in India has mostly stayed inside DRDO and the public sector. A private company setting up end-to-end missile manufacturing at this scale hasn’t really happened before. It widens the base of who can actually build this stuff, which matters if India wants supply chains that don’t buckle under a single point of failure.
DRDO and HAL have begun structural load studies on the Su-30MKI’s nose radome, the protective cone housing the aircraft’s radar, to prepare for the fitting of the new indigenous Virupaksha AESA radar. Engineers are testing how the radome holds up under high speed and high-angle manoeuvres, since even a slight flex could throw off the radar’s accuracy. It’s not just the radar either, this sits inside a bigger upgrade package for the Su-30MKI that also includes new mission computers, updated electronic warfare systems, and integration with the Astra Mk-3 missile and BrahMos, all aimed at pushing the fleet closer to 4.5-generation capability.
Why it matters : The Su-30MKI makes up the largest chunk of the IAF’s fighter fleet, over 250 aircraft, and all of them are currently flying with radar technology that’s decades old at this point. An AESA radar changes what these jets can actually do in a fight, better jamming resistance, more targets tracked at once, and a much better chance of picking up stealth aircraft. This is the difference between retiring the fleet in ten years or keeping it frontline for twenty.
DRDO test-fired the Pinaka Long Range Guided Rocket at Chandipur on July 8, hitting a target 60 km out. The trajectory matched predictions closely enough that officials called it a textbook run. The rocket was fired using the Army’s existing Pinaka launcher, no new equipment needed. Rajnath Singh described it as a major step for India’s long-range rocket capability.
Why it matters : The launcher compatibility is really the point here. The same system already in service can now fire multiple Pinaka variants across different ranges, so the Army adds strike depth without procuring anything new. For units stationed along the LAC and LoC, that’s a meaningful jump in how far and how precisely they can hit targets.
Four Indian companies, Lokesh Machines, RRG Engineering Technologies, Galaxy Bearings and Shaurya Aeronautics, are off the US Treasury’s sanctions list after being designated back in October 2024 over alleged links to Russia’s defence supply chain. What’s notable isn’t just the removal, it’s the speed. These delistings typically take five to six years to work through. This one took 20 months, driven by a combination of MEA and NSCS diplomatic pressure and US legal counsel that three of the four firms hired to fight their case directly.
Why it matters : This is the first time an Indian company has come off an OFAC Russia-sanctions list since the 2024 crackdown began, and that’s the real story here, not the four firms themselves. India’s defence industry has one foot in old Russian-origin supply chains and the other in a fast-growing US tech relationship, a position that was always going to create friction like this. What just happened gives every other Indian firm caught in that same bind an actual precedent to point to, proof that this is fixable, and roughly how long it takes.
Trump told reporters at the Nato summit in Ankara that the US will lift sanctions on Turkey and may readmit it to the F-35 programme, seven years after Washington expelled Ankara for buying Russia’s S-400 missile system. Turkey never gave up the S-400. Under US law, that alone blocks the F-35 sale. Congress has not signalled any appetite to change that. Israel has objected too, arguing a Turkish F-35 fleet would erode its regional air advantage. Separately, Trump has already approved Turkey’s purchase of F110 jet engines.
Why it matters : The F-35 is the single biggest lever Trump has to pull Ankara back into Washington’s orbit. But Congress, not Trump, controls the certification that Turkey no longer has the S-400, and Erdogan has given no indication he plans to part with it. A workaround, if one emerges, would be the clearest test yet of how far the US will stretch its own sanctions law for a NATO member that keeps one foot in Moscow. India faced the identical CAATSA problem over its S-400 purchase and settled for a waiver rather than a fix, so this outcome carries a direct precedent for New Delhi.
A Russian Tu-142 Bear-F patrol plane flew low past HMS Prince of Wales in the Norwegian Sea on July 2, close enough that it dropped a string of sonobuoys near the carrier and didn’t respond when the UK radioed it. Two F-35Bs scrambled off the ship to intercept and see it off. London called it unsafe. This wasn’t a one-off either, Nato says Russian naval activity near UK waters has jumped 30 percent over the last two years, and these Bear flybys have basically become routine at this point, Russia testing how fast a carrier group reacts and what its radar picks up.
Nato has settled on Saab’s GlobalEye as its next airborne early warning plane, with 11 members, including Germany, Canada, the Netherlands and Sweden, signing up to buy roughly ten of them together. Boeing’s E-7 Wedgetail was the original pick, but the US pulled out of the programme last year over cost and shifting priorities, leaving GlobalEye as effectively the only Western jet-based option left standing. GlobalEye works by combining Saab’s Erieye radar with sensors that also track ships and ground movement, all mounted on a Bombardier business jet, and it can stay in the air for over 11 hours at a time.
Canada has picked Germany’s ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems to build up to 12 new Type 212CD submarines, replacing its ageing Victoria-class fleet. PM Mark Carney called it the biggest defence purchase in Canadian history. Canada is joining Germany and Norway’s existing production line, with first delivery expected by 2034. The 212CD runs on hydrogen fuel cells, letting it stay submerged far longer than a standard diesel-electric boat. Germany beat out a South Korean bid for the contract.
The deal is as much about Nato burden-sharing as submarines. Canada has lagged on defence spending for years, and this is Ottawa’s signal that it’s serious about hitting Nato’s 5 percent GDP target by 2035. For Germany, it cements TKMS as Europe’s dominant conventional submarine builder, already supplying over a third of Nato members. It’s relevant to India too: TKMS is one of two shortlisted bidders, alongside Spain’s Navantia, for Project-75I, so the terms Berlin offered Canada are worth watching as those talks continue.
Britain and the Netherlands will build eight new amphibious transport ships together under a £2.4 billion agreement signed this week, four for each navy. The design comes from the Dutch, but construction will happen in UK yards, the ships are meant to move troops, vehicles and drones. Britain has been without a proper amphibious fleet since HMS Albion and Bulwark went to Brazil after being retired in 2024. This deal fills that gap.
Sharing the build with the Netherlands brings the cost down and locks in interoperability between two navies that already train together under the Joint Expeditionary Force. UK yards have taken this kind of allied order before, most recently the Type 26 frigate deal with Norway. The pattern is becoming familiar: British shipbuilding isn’t chasing full independence after Brexit so much as embedding itself in NATO co-production arrangements it can rely on for repeat work.
Egypt just opened a new military command centre called The Octagon, built in its new capital city east of Cairo. It’s enormous, roughly 22,000 acres across eight connected octagon-shaped buildings, bigger in footprint than the Pentagon. President Sissi called it a major upgrade to how Egypt runs its command and control, and the building brings the Army, Navy, Air Force, intelligence agencies and civilian government functions together under one roof, tied into AI-linked systems. Egypt has also been a growing defence partner for India in recent years, from joint air exercises to interest from Cairo in platforms like Tejas and BrahMos, so a more centralised, modernised Egyptian command structure is a relevant data point for India’s own push to widen its defence-export footprint across the Middle East and North Africa.
Reports suggest India wants to restart the Chabahar-Zahedan rail line, a 700-km stretch through Iran that’s been talked about for nearly a decade but never actually built. The reason it’s back on the table now is Iran. Washington and Tehran appear to have reached some kind of understanding that loosens sanctions, and part of that reportedly includes India resuming crude oil purchases from Iran, something that stopped almost seven years ago. Nothing here is official yet, no announcement, no signed agreement, no dates. But the direction is clear enough that it’s worth tracking.
The rail line itself would connect Chabahar port to Zahedan, and from Zahedan into Iran’s existing network, which eventually links up with the International North-South Transport Corridor running toward Central Asia and Russia. The whole appeal of this route for India has always been that it avoids Pakistan completely.
Why it matters : India has spent money and diplomatic effort on Chabahar since 2016, mainly to get into Afghanistan and Central Asia without going through Pakistan. But a port is only as useful as what connects to it. Chabahar has had cargo moving out by truck, which was never going to be enough to justify the investment. A rail line changes that. It’s what turns Chabahar from a talking point into something India can actually run trade through, a real alternative to Gwadar rather than just a rival to it on paper.
INS Sudarshini completed her New York port call on July 8, part of Lokayan 2026, the Navy’s 10-month sail training deployment. She took part in the Parade of Sail marking 250 years of American independence, sailing past the Statue of Liberty on the Hudson, and opened her decks to over 1,000 visitors in Brooklyn, many from the Indian diaspora there. She now heads to Boston for Sail Boston 2026.
Indian and Rwandan defence officials sat down in Delhi on July 6 and 7 for their second Joint Defence Cooperation Committee meeting, and came out of it with plans to widen training exchanges, joint exercises, military medical cooperation, and defence-industry ties, all on a fixed timeline this time round. Rwanda’s delegation also got a tour of India’s defence production ecosystem and a stop at Army Hospital in Delhi, and met Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh. The relationship itself isn’t new, it traces back to a defence MoU signed in 2018.

Heading: SDM becomes hero of Operation Sindoor, honored by Army Chief himself
Summary:
• SDM Satish Sharma of Khour sub-division was honored by Army Chief General Dheeraj Seth for his leadership during 'Operation Sindoor'.
• Sharma successfully coordinated the evacuation of over 73,000 civilians from 53 border villages with zero casualties.
• His proactive administration and field presence ensured effective relief, medical support, and timely compensation for affected families in Jammu and Kashmir.
Content: Akhnoor (Rohit Mishra): Chief of Army Staff (COAS) General Dheeraj Seth honored SDM Khour, Satish Sharma, on the spot for his excellent administration during 'Operation Sindoor'. Satish Sharma, a dedicated and professional government officer currently serving as SDM of Khour sub-division, played a crucial role in the operation. Due to his active leadership and meticulous planning, he successfully evacuated civilians from 53 border villages within an 8km radius. Under his supervision, Village Action Teams (VATs) were formed, medical infrastructure was strengthened, transport was arranged, and relief camps were provided with food, sanitation, and healthcare. A 24x7 control room was established for real-time coordination between agencies. Through his efforts, over 73,000 out of 86,000 people were safely evacuated, and 17,000 were sheltered in camps, with zero casualties in the Khour sub-division. Satish Sharma personally visited sensitive areas despite shelling and communication hurdles, working round-the-clock. His proactive actions saved at least 80 lives, including those whose homes were destroyed. After the evacuation, he conducted a detailed survey of property and livestock damage alongside army personnel and oversaw the distribution of government compensation to affected families.

Heading: AI may shape future wars, but victory will depend on soldiers, national resolve: Rajnath Singh
Summary: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, while commissioning INS Mahendragiri in Visakhapatnam, stated that while AI is transforming warfare, victory in future conflicts will rely on national resolve and trained soldiers. He emphasized balancing technological advancements with conventional military strength and highlighted how indigenous warship construction boosts India's industrial ecosystem, economy, and maritime security under the Maritime India Vision 2030.
Content:
Visakhapatnam, July 11 (IANS):Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday asserted that while emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence are transforming the nature of warfare, conventional military capabilities remain indispensable, stressing that future conflicts may involve AI but will ultimately be won through national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military strength.

Addressing the gathering during the commissioning ceremony of INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy in Andhra Pradesh's Visakhapatnam, Defence Minister Singh said, "While new technologies have certainly transformed the nature of warfare, they have not diminished the importance of conventional warfare capabilities. Strong conventional capabilities remain just as essential today as ever for fulfilling the fundamental principles of warfare. Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won through national resolve, trained soldiers, and credible military power."

Highlighting the need to balance technological advancement with conventional strength, the Defence Minister said, "New technology and conventional platforms are not adversaries but complements to one another; a conventional platform is incomplete without new technology, and a conventional platform is weakened without it. History bears witness that nations which neglected their conventional strength, lured by the appeal of new technology, had to pay a heavy price."

Emphasising India's long-term defence strategy, Defence Minister Singh said, "Therefore, India's approach is very clear: We must excel in both areas and maintain a balance between them."

"We will invest in future technologies while continuously honing our conventional capabilities. INS Mahendragiri stands as a symbol of this very resolve and commitment," he added.

Referring to India's recent military operations, the Defence Minister said the country's ability to effectively integrate conventional and modern capabilities had already been demonstrated.

"In recent times, we have also witnessed how our conventional and modern capabilities work in tandem when it comes to national security. 'Operation Sindoor' was a prime example of this. During that operation, our armed forces demonstrated that India is fully capable not only of self-defence but also of delivering a decisive response and completely eliminating the enemy when the need arises," he said.

Defence Minister Singh further stated that every warship commissioned into the Navy contributes to strengthening India's broader defence and industrial ecosystem.

"With every ship, India's ecosystem matures, becomes more efficient, and grows more confident."

Explaining the wider economic significance of indigenous warship construction, he said, "That is why I believe that every new ship represents a long-term investment in India's maritime future. The construction of a warship is not merely the building of a vessel; it entails the creation of an entire industrial ecosystem."

"The shipbuilding industry drives progress across sectors such as steel, electronics, sensors, propulsion systems, software, precision engineering, logistics, and numerous ancillary industries. This generates employment opportunities for lakhs of people, fosters the development of new technologies, and imparts fresh momentum to our economy. Thus, when we build a ship, we not only strengthen our Navy but also infuse new energy into India's economic prowess," he added.

The Defence Minister also said India has an ambitious pipeline of naval projects planned for the coming years, with the objective of positioning the country as a global centre for shipbuilding and maritime defence innovation.

"I am confident that, in the near future, our country will carve a distinct niche for itself among the world's leading nations in this sector. We aim to move forward in collaboration with domestic industries, the private sector, MSMEs, startups, innovators, and our global partners. Driven by this vision, our government is working rapidly on the 'Maritime India Vision 2030'," he said.

He further highlighted the government's policy initiatives aimed at strengthening the maritime sector.

"The government has launched several significant initiatives, such as the Maritime Development Fund, the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Scheme, and the Shipbuilding Development Scheme. These efforts will strengthen our industrial base, expand our shipbuilding capacity, and correspondingly bolster our maritime capabilities to safeguard India's growing economic interests," Singh added.

Content:
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Thursday accused the BJP of increasing India's economic dependence on China despite the 2020 Galwan clash, alleging that Beijing has gained a dominant position in several strategic sectors under the current administration.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, citing a media report and official trade data, claimed that Chinese imports had expanded significantly across industries critical to India's economy, including pharmaceuticals, electric vehicles and renewable energy.
"Six years ago, PM Narendra Modi handed over a clean chit to China after our 20 brave soldiers made the supreme sacrifice in Galwan. Our bravehearts chose martyrdom, but the Modi government has surrendered India's interests to China," Kharge said in a post on X.
Kharge alleged that India's imports from China had risen by 101.81 per cent since the Galwan clash, pushing the bilateral trade deficit to USD 112.1 billion in 2025-26.
He claimed China supplied 86 per cent of India's antibiotic imports and accounted for nearly 74 per cent of imports of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), bulk drugs and drug intermediates during 2024-25.
The Congress chief also alleged that 66 per cent of India's electric vehicle component imports originated from China, while nearly three-fourths of imported lithium-ion batteries used in Indian EVs were Chinese.
He further claimed that China supplied around 93 per cent of India's permanent magnet imports in 2025-26.
On the renewable energy sector, Kharge alleged that China supplied more than 99 per cent of India's undiffused silicon wafer imports in 2025-26, calling it a near-total dominance of a sector that the government has identified as central to its Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative.
The Congress leader also criticised the Centre's reported decision to allow four Chinese companies to bid for government power projects, alleging that it had "rolled out the red carpet" for what he referred to as PM Modi's "Jhoola Friend".
He further alleged that China continued to encroach on Indian territory in Arunachal Pradesh and Ladakh and claimed Beijing's role in Pakistan's actions during Operation Sindoor had been acknowledged by the Deputy Chief of Army Staff.
"Modi government has hurt India's national interests by letting Beijing capture India's most critical industries since Galwan. Now they are opening more opportunities for the Chinese to flourish under the lens of his tinted 'Laal Aankh'!" Kharge said.
There was no immediate response from the Centre or the Bharatiya Janata Party to the Congress' allegations.

Now they are opening more opportunities for the Chinese to flourish under the lens of his tinted 'Laal Aankh'," he said. Earlier in June, Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu rejected Beijing's territorial claims over the state, asserting that Arunachal Pradesh is an integral part of India. The Indian Army has also dismissed reports alleging fresh Chinese encroachment in Arunachal Pradesh, describing them as "incorrect and without any basis."

- Kharge cited significant surges in imports from China in antibiotics, EV components, and solar manufacturing, pushing the bilateral trade deficit.
- He also alleged Chinese encroachment in Arunachal Pradesh and Ladakh, claiming the Modi government compromised India's national interests.
Content: Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday launched a sharp attack on the Narendra Modi-led government, alleging that India has become increasingly dependent on China across several strategic sectors despite the 2020 Galwan Valley clash, and accused the Centre of compromising the country's national interests. In a post on social media platform X marking six years since the Galwan Valley clash, Kharge said Prime Minister Narendra Modi/ had given China a "clean chit" after the deaths of 20 Indian soldiers in the violent border confrontation. "Six years ago, PM @narendramodi handed over a CLEAN CHIT to China, after our 20 brave soldiers made the supreme sacrifice in Galwan. Our bravehearts chose martyrdom, but the Modi Government has surrendered India's interests to China," Kharge said. The Congress chief alleged that India's dependence on China now runs through some of the country's most critical economic sectors and claimed that imports from China have surged significantly since the Galwan clash. Citing trade figures, Kharge claimed that India's imports from China had increased by 101.81 per cent by 2025-26, pushing the bilateral trade deficit to $112.1 billion. He further alleged that China accounted for 86 per cent of India's antibiotic imports and nearly 74 per cent of imports of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), bulk drugs and drug intermediates during 2024-25. Turning to the electric vehicle sector, Kharge claimed that 66 per cent of India's EV component imports continued to come from China, while nearly 75 per cent of lithium-ion batteries used in Indian electric vehicles were imported, with the overwhelming majority sourced from Chinese manufacturers. He also alleged that India imported nearly 93 per cent of its permanent magnets from China during 2025-26. The Congress president also criticised the government's renewable energy policy, alleging that despite its emphasis on self-reliance under the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative, China supplied more than 99 per cent of India's undiffused silicon wafer imports in 2025-26, which he described as the foundation of solar cell manufacturing. Kharge further alleged that the government had relaxed restrictions to allow four Chinese companies to bid for government power projects, accusing the Prime Minister of rolling out the "red carpet" for his "Jhoola Friend." Referring to national security concerns, the Congress leader said reports from civil society organisations indicated that China continued to encroach upon Indian territory in Arunachal Pradesh and Ladakh. He also claimed that China's role in supporting Pakistan during Operation Sindoor had been acknowledged by the Deputy Chief of Army Staff and was officially documented. "Modi Government has hurt India's national interests by letting Beijing capture India's most critical industries since Galwan. Now they are opening more opportunities for the Chinese to flourish," Kharge said. The remarks come amid continuing political exchanges between the ruling BJP and the Congress over the government's handling of relations with China following the Galwan Valley clash of June 2020, in which 20 Indian soldiers lost their lives. The incident marked the deadliest confrontation between Indian and Chinese troops along the Line of Actual Control in decades and triggered a series of diplomatic, military and economic measures by India, including restrictions on several Chinese mobile applications, tighter scrutiny of investments from neighbouring countries and efforts to diversify critical supply chains. The BJP has consistently maintained that the government has taken firm measures to safeguard India's territorial integrity and strengthen domestic manufacturing, while the Congress has repeatedly questioned the government's China policy and alleged that economic dependence on Beijing has continued to deepen despite official claims of promoting self-reliance.

Content: According to news agency ANI, speaking to reporters on Air Force One at RAF Mildenhall in the UK, Trump said, "Just imagine - there was a war going on between India and Pakistan." Heading: Trump reiterated: "I stopped India and Pakistan's nuclear war, declared myself worthy of the Nobel Prize."
Summary: Former US President Donald Trump has reiterated his claim of preventing a nuclear war between India and Pakistan in May, stating that the conflict could have resulted in millions of deaths and that he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts. He claimed to have resolved eight wars, including the India-Pakistan conflict, by threatening tariffs.
