Opposition parties are also expected to raise privilege action against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh over alleged misleading statements regarding soldier deaths, alongside addressing internal party rebellions and the strengthening political position of the ruling NDA.
Content: NEW DELHI: Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced that the Parliament Monsoon Session will be held from the 20th of this month until the 13th of next month. "These sessions will commence on July 20 and continue until August 13 for meaningful discussions and decisions on issues of national importance," he revealed on 'X' platform on Saturday. He stated that the Monsoon Session will have 19 sittings over a total of 25 days. Meanwhile, the Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) examining the controversial 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill is likely to approve its report on the 17th of this month. Indications are that the most debated provision in the bill, which suggests removing the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers, Union or State Ministers from office if arrested in serious criminal cases and held in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days, is likely to be retained. However, there are also chances that some safeguards will be included in this report with the aim of preventing the misuse of this provision for political vendetta. Furthermore, in the wake of Congress alleging that Defence Minister Rajnath Singh told a 'direct and clear lie' to mislead the House regarding the deaths of Indian soldiers during Operation Sindoor, opposition parties are likely to raise the issue of privilege action against him. The developments of rebellions within the Trinamool Congress (TMC) and Shiv Sena (UBT) are likely to impact the upcoming sessions. Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla needs to decide on the demands made by 20 TMC and six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs seeking recognition as separate groups. These sessions are set to take place at a time when the political strength of the ruling NDA has further increased after newly elected and re-elected MPs took oath in the Rajya Sabha. Additionally, with three rebel TMC MPs from the Upper House resigning and by-elections in the Rajya Sabha, the BJP is set to gain further strength.

Heading: Opposition to seek discussion on NEET, inflation during Parliament's Monsoon session: Imran Masood
Summary: The Opposition, led by Congress MP Imran Masood, plans to seek discussions on the NEET controversy and rising inflation during the upcoming Monsoon Session of Parliament, scheduled from July 20 to August 13. Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju confirmed the session dates, which are expected to see heated debates, including potential privilege proceedings against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. Meanwhile, the re-NEET-UG results are anticipated by July 20, just before the session begins.
Content: New Delhi [India], July 5 (ANI): The Opposition will seek a discussion on the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test ( NEET ) controversy and rising inflation during the upcoming Monsoon Session of Parliament , Congress Lok Sabha MP Imran Masood said. Masood said NEET and inflation would be among the Opposition's primary concerns during the session, which is scheduled to begin on July 20. "The biggest issue is NEET . The second issue is inflation in the country. These are major issues. We would want the government to discuss them, but we know the government will run away from discussion. The government does not want to hold discussions... The government is weak," Masood told ANI on Saturday.. His remarks came a day after Union Parliament ary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced that the Monsoon Session of Parliament will be held from July 20 to August 13. In a post on X, Rijiju said that President Droupadi Murmu had approved the government's recommendation to summon both Houses of Parliament for the session. "On the recommendation of the Govt of India, Hon'ble President, Smt. Droupadi Murmu ji has approved the summoning of both the Houses of Parliament for the Monsoon Session 2026. The Session will commence on July 20, 2026 and continue till August 13, 2026, for meaningful debate, discussion and decisions on issues of National Importance," Rijiju said. The Monsoon Session is expected to witness heated exchanges between the Treasury and Opposition benches over a range of issues. Apart from NEET and inflation, the Opposition is likely to raise the issue of privilege proceedings against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh over his statements on casualties during Operation Sindoor. The Joint Parliament ary Committee (JPC) examining the proposed 130th Constitution Amendment Bill is also expected to adopt its report on July 17 before submitting it to Parliament . The Bill has sparked political debate over a provision that mandates the automatic removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Union or State ministers from office if they remain in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days in cases involving serious offences. Meanwhile, the National Testing Agency (NTA) has said the results of the re- NEET -UG examination, conducted on June 21 following the cancellation of the earlier test over the alleged paper leak, will be declared by July 20, ahead of the commencement of the Monsoon Session . (ANI)

Heading: Parliament Monsoon Session from 20th
Summary: The Parliament Monsoon Session is scheduled from July 20th to August 13th, lasting 19 days, as announced by Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju. Key discussions are anticipated, including a report on the removal of a High Court judge, a redrafted bill for women's reservation and increased Lok Sabha seats, and a proposed law regarding ministers losing office if convicted. The sessions are expected to be contentious, with issues like a privilege motion against the Defence Minister also likely to create a stir.
Content:
Delhi: The Parliament Monsoon Session will begin on the 20th of this month and continue until August 13. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju officially announced on Saturday that it will last for 19 days. These are the first sessions after the BJP's victory in the recent assembly elections. This is also the first time Parliament is convening after a split among Trinamool Congress and Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs. Speaker Om Birla is yet to decide on the request by 20 Trinamool and six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs to be recognized separately. After the election of new members, the numerical strength in the Rajya Sabha is shifting in favor of the NDA. Speaker Om Birla informed reporters in Kolkata on Saturday that the report submitted by the three-member committee appointed for the removal of High Court Judge Justice Yashwant Varma, following the discovery of burnt currency notes at his home, will be presented in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon Session. He stated that further action would be taken after members discuss the report. Although Justice Varma has resigned from his post, the President has not yet accepted it.

This time, the sessions are expected to be heated. The constitutional amendment bill introduced last time in the Lok Sabha, which proposed implementing women's reservations in legislatures only from 2029 and increasing Lok Sabha seats, failed. The government is redrafting the bill to increase seats by 50% in all states. Southern states are clearly stating that increasing seats based on population is not appropriate.

Issues such as a proposed law that would cause even the Prime Minister to lose office if convicted of criminal charges and not granted bail within 30 days, and the notice given by Congress against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh for alleged breach of privilege – stating that no soldiers died in 'Operation Sindoor' in Parliament previously but recently announcing the names of the deceased – are expected to create a stir.

Heading: Confidence in Indian-made defense equipment increased after Operation Sindoor: Union Minister Rajnath Singh
Summary: Union Minister Rajnath Singh stated that global confidence in Indian-made defense equipment has significantly increased following India's Operation Sindoor against terrorist camps in Pakistan and PoK. He highlighted a remarkable 57-fold growth in defense exports, from Rs. 686 crore in 2013-14 to Rs. 38,000 crore currently, alongside a substantial increase in domestic production. Singh emphasized India's journey from scarcity to self-sufficiency and self-confidence, now aiming for a developed nation, while also discussing the importance of human emotional intelligence over AI's data analysis capabilities.
Content:
"Confidence in Indian-made defense equipment has increased after Operation Sindoor," said Defense Minister Rajnath Singh.
Participating in an event in Delhi on Saturday, Rajnath Singh further spoke about this:
After India's Operation Sindoor against terrorist camps located in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir following the Pahalgam terrorist attack, global confidence in Indian-made defense equipment has increased.
Many countries are purchasing Indian products. Defense equipment exports, which were merely Rs. 686 crore in 2013-14, have now reached a record level of Rs. 38,000 crore. This is a 57-fold growth.
Defense equipment production has also increased. Production, which was valued at Rs. 46,000 crore 8 to 9 years ago, has now reached Rs. 1.78 lakh crore.
India's journey over the last 12 years has been from scarcity to self-sufficiency, and from self-sufficiency to self-confidence. It is now moving towards the goal of a developed India.
While giving importance to technological development, India also cherishes its traditions. The combination of technology and tradition serves as India's biggest bridge in the 21st century, he said.
He also pointed out that "Artificial Intelligence (AI) has permeated all aspects of human life, and while AI can analyze data, it cannot understand human emotions or know their state of mind. That is where the human emotional approach becomes important."

Heading: Op Sindoor boosted trust in Indian defence platforms : Rajnath Singh
Summary: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh stated that Operation Sindoor significantly boosted trust in "made-in-India" defence platforms, citing a substantial increase in India's defence production and exports. He also highlighted India's progress towards self-reliance and a 'Viksit Bharat' through a blend of tradition and technology. Singh further emphasized the crucial role of human sensitivity, credibility, and accuracy in journalism, particularly when reporting on national security matters, despite advancements in AI.
Content:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday said that after Operation Sindoor, the trust in “made-in-India” defence platforms has received a boost.

In his address at an event in New Delhi, he also reiterated that “today, our defence production has reached over Rs 1.78 lakh crore, and about 8-9 years ago, it stood at approximately Rs 46,000 crore”. The Union Minister asserted that after Operation Sindoor, “trust in made-in-India defence platforms has been enhanced”.

Operation Sindoor was India’s decisive military action conducted in May 2025 in response to the Pahalgam terror attack. Several defence platforms built in India had played a key role in it.

Singh said, “Defence exports too have reached a record over Rs 38,000 crore, and in 2013-14, it stood at just Rs 686 crore, and it has grown today 57 times. And, I have not sought the full report, but currently it should be hovering around Rs 40,000 crore, which is my estimate.”

In his address, he also spoke of India’s journey in various sectors in the last 12 years, the advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and the importance of human sensitivity in the age of AI, including in the field of journalism.

The event was hosted in Delhi to mark 80 years of the national Hindi daily Navbharat Times.

“India’s journey over the last 12 years has been a progression from shortages to self-reliance, from self-reliance to self-confidence, and from self-confidence towards building a Viksit Bharat,” Singh said.

He said India lays emphasis on both technological development and celebrating its traditions, and this confluence of “tradition and technology” is the “biggest strength of the country in the 21st century”.

Underlining that AI has touched nearly all aspects of human existence today, he cautioned that while AI can read and analyse data, it “cannot feel the pulse” of the people, which is where human sensitivity comes into the picture.

Singh pointed out that journalism, too, has been impacted by technological advancements such as AI, but they won’t be able to surpass human creativity and intellect.

“The future success of journalism will depend on how well it establishes the balance and synergy between the capabilities of AI and human empathy. While AI will make journalism faster and more precise, emotional intelligence will ensure that it remains humane and credible,” he said. The Union Minister also emphasised maintaining credibility in journalism in the era of fake news and misinformation.

Terming the media’s role in the present era of what he described as “communicative abundance” as more crucial than ever, the defence minister said the challenge today is not a lack of information, but its accuracy and reliability.

Misinformation severely impacts society and the morale of defence forces, he said, adding that while being the first to report may be important in journalism, disseminating correct news is even more crucial.

“Especially when the subject concerns the defence forces, national security, or the honour of those who make the supreme sacrifice in the service of the nation, every word becomes a matter of national responsibility. The media must always uphold the values of accuracy, objectivity, and impartiality,” Singh said.

Heading: Women's reservation may be brought up again during Monsoon Session": BJP MP Manan Kumar Mishra
Summary: BJP MP Manan Kumar Mishra anticipates discussions on the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam 2023 (women's reservation) and the 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill (PM-CM Bill) during the upcoming Monsoon Session, citing shifts in parliamentary numbers due to recent party splits. While government-aligned MPs hope for a productive session, RJD MP Manoj Jha criticizes the party splits as a "betrayal of the electorate's mandate" and plans to raise issues like alleged donation embezzlement and foreign policy concerns. The opposition also intends to bring up privilege proceedings against the Defence Minister.
Content: New Delhi [India], July 4 (ANI): BJP Rajya Sabha MP Manan Kumar Mishra on Saturday said that the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam 2023 is expected to be discussed again in the upcoming Monsoon Session of Parliament after the splits in the Trinamool Congress and Shiv Sena (UBT) have changed the numbers for the NDA in the Houses. The Monsoon Session of Parliament will be held from July 20 to August 13, Union Parliament ary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said. Speaking to ANI, Mishra also said that the Centre is expected to table the 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill, which provides for the automatic removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Union or State ministers from office if they are arrested and remain in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days in cases involving serious offences. The Rajya Sabha MP acknowledged that 20 TMC MPs merging with the NCPI, six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs joining the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena, and seven Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) Rajya Sabha MPs merging with the BJP have made the NDA closer to the two-thirds majority in the Houses to get the Constitutional amendments passed. He also took into consideration the rift between the DMK and Congress, after the latter quit the regional alliance and joined hands with the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) in Tamil Nadu. He said, "Although the agenda hasn't been presented to us yet, that is something the Minister of Parliament ary Affairs decides. But based on our rough assessment, we expect the issue of 33 per cent women's reservation to be brought up again. Circumstances have changed significantly: we won in West Bengal, there has been a split within the TMC, the situation in Maharashtra has shifted, and the stance of the DMK has also changed." "Given this situation, we expect measures regarding women's reservation and delimitation, and then there is the 130th Constitutional Amendment, often referred to as the 'PM-CM Bill', which entails automatic removal from office; if a Minister or Chief Minister remains in jail for more than 30 days, they would automatically vacate their office. Following that, issues concerning national security will be discussed; these are important items of business. We expect these to come up during the Monsoon Session," the BJP leader added. During the special session of Parliament held on April 16-18, the Constitutional Amendment Bill aiming to increase the number of Lok Sabha seats and operationalise the women's reservation law was defeated in the Lok Sabha. For the 130th Constitution Amendment Bill, a Joint Parliament ary Committee (JPC) examining the controversial legislation is expected to adopt its report on July 17. Rajya Sabha MP Ghulam Ali Khatana said, "This session is part of the regular schedule, which we call the Monsoon Session, and we hope that both the ruling party and the opposition will bring forward matters beneficial to the common people and raise their issues. We also hope that both Houses remain fully functional throughout the session, conducting debates and discussions without arrogance or disruptions." Meanwhile, RJD MP Manoj Jha lashed out at the Centre following the splits in the TMC and UBT Sena, terming them a "betrayal of the electorate's mandate." He said that the Opposition will raise the issue in the Parliament in the upcoming session. The Opposition is also expected to corner the Centre on alleged donation embezzlement in the Ayodhya Ram Temple and bring up privilege proceedings against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, accusing him of misleading the House over casualties of Indian soldiers during Operation Sindoor. Manoj Jha said, "They try to use Parliament merely as a rubber stamp. When Parliament isn't in session, they engage in the engineering of splits within parties, which amounts to a betrayal of the Indian electorate's mandate. Fraud doesn't just happen with Ram Mandir donations; it happens to the Indian voter. Are they ready to discuss this? There are many issues which we wanted to discuss. Does the government have any clue regarding issues of equality? Do they have any idea about anything, from the theft of donations to employment?" "Will the government be willing to openly discuss the wavering stance on foreign policy, the consequences of which we have witnessed from February until now? We will also ask what happened to the Pulwama report and the Pahalgam report; how far did those investigations progress, and who was at fault? Who is accountable? Who is responsible? These are all crucial questions which we wanted to ask," the RJD MP added. (ANI)

Heading: Monsoon Session of Parliament from July 20: Minister Kiren Rijiju
Summary: Union Minister Kiren Rijiju announced that the Monsoon Session of Parliament will run from July 20 to August 13, focusing on national issues. A key agenda item is the controversial 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill, which proposes automatic disqualification for ministers in judicial custody for 30 days, a provision the JPC is likely to retain with added safeguards. Additionally, opposition parties are expected to move a privilege motion against Defense Minister Rajnath Singh over alleged false statements.
Content:
New Delhi, July 4: Union Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju announced on Saturday that the Monsoon Session of Parliament will commence from July 20.
He stated in an X post that the session will begin on July 20 and continue until August 13, for meaningful discussions, debates, and decisions on matters of national importance.
According to a news agency report, the Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) reviewing the controversial 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill is likely to adopt its report on July 17. There are indications that the committee will retain the most debated provision in the bill, which states that if the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers, and central or state ministers are arrested in serious criminal cases and remain in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days, they will automatically lose their office.
Another meeting of the committee has been called on July 17. Although several parties expressed concerns during consultations, the committee is unlikely to recommend dropping this controversial provision. However, sources indicate that the report is expected to include necessary safeguards to prevent the misuse of this provision for political vendetta or motivated lawsuits.
The proposed amendment has sparked intense political debate. While supporters argue that it strengthens accountability in public office, opposition parties have warned that it could be used to destabilize elected governments through politically motivated investigations and arrests.
After the JPC finalizes and adopts its report in its July 17 meeting, it is expected to be submitted to Parliament for further consideration.
Opposition parties are also likely to raise the issue of initiating privilege motion proceedings against Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, following allegations by the Congress that he made completely false statements about Indian soldiers' casualties during ‘Operation Sindoor’ to mislead the House.

Heading: Opposition Prepares to Weaponize Rajnath's Statement on Operation Sindoor, Monsoon Session to See Uproar
Summary: The upcoming Monsoon Session of Parliament is anticipated to be contentious, with the opposition planning to challenge Defence Minister Rajnath Singh's statement on Operation Sindoor, accusing him of misleading the House regarding soldier casualties. Another key focus will be the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025, which proposes the automatic removal of a PM, CM, or minister if held in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days, a provision facing both support for accountability and criticism for potentially altering the constitutional structure. The BJP is also working to increase its strength in both Houses to pass such constitutional amendments, which have proven challenging in the past.
Content:
The dates for the Monsoon Session of Parliament have been announced, and it is certain to be a tumultuous session. The opposition has made its preparations, with Defence Minister Rajnath Singh's statement on Operation Sindoor being their biggest weapon. Additionally, the opposition is likely to attack some controversial proposals by the BJP government. Under one such proposal, a Prime Minister, Chief Minister, or minister would be removed from office if they remain in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days. The government announced on Saturday that the Monsoon Session will run from July 20 to August 13. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju stated that President Droupadi Murmu has accepted the proposal.

Controversy over Rajnath Singh's statement: The opposition may adopt an aggressive stance on Rajnath Singh's statement regarding Operation Sindoor. Last year, during a discussion on Operation Sindoor in the House, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh claimed that not a single Indian soldier was scratched during the operation. In contrast, some time ago, the government stated that six Indian soldiers were martyred during Operation Sindoor. The Congress, during the recent INDIA alliance meeting, accused Rajnath Singh of misleading the House on this matter. Congress General Secretary KC Venugopal has issued a privilege motion notice against the minister, accusing him of lying in Parliament.

Focus on JPC Report: This parliamentary session is expected to focus on the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025. The Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) investigating this law is scheduled to meet on July 17 to finalize its report. It is believed that the JPC will likely not recommend removing the controversial provision of the bill. According to this provision, in cases of serious crimes, if a PM, CM, and central or state minister are arrested and remain in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days, there will be a provision for their automatic removal. Furthermore, PM Narendra Modi's government could not pass a constitutional amendment in the previous session due to a lack of the necessary numbers in Parliament.

Arguments of Supporters and Critics: Supporters and critics are presenting different arguments regarding the provision to remove PMs and CMs from office. Supporters argue that allowing leaders to be removed based on imprisonment, even if only on charges, will increase accountability in public offices. However, critics say that this would fundamentally alter the constitutional structure. Opposition parties fear that this proposal could prove dangerous.

Significant Challenges Ahead: Even if the JPC submits its report before Parliament reconvenes, this law will face more challenges than an ordinary bill. Since it seeks to amend the Constitution, according to Article 368 of the Constitution, this bill must be passed separately by a 'special majority' in both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. This requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting in each House. This amendment directly affects constitutional provisions related to executive positions, so it is expected to be approved by the President and by the legislatures of at least half of the states before becoming effective.

BJP's Focus on Increasing Strength: There is much discussion about this arithmetic. In view of this, the BJP is focusing on increasing its strength in both Houses. This includes electoral victories, defections within parties, and the use of regional parties. The party is also trying to advance other constitutional measures, including laws related to delimitation and the Women's Reservation Bill. The 131st amendment proposal, which failed to pass in Parliament in April, clearly indicates that the BJP or NDA currently lacks sufficient numbers for major changes. Thus, the 130th Amendment Bill, which includes provisions for removing PMs, CMs, and ministers, has become a major test for the government.

Heading: Rajnath Singh Under Fire: What Is Operation Sindoor Casualty Row?
Summary: The Congress party has intensified its criticism of Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, accusing him of misleading Parliament regarding casualties in Operation Sindoor after the government disclosed the names of six military personnel killed. The party has filed a privilege motion and demanded Singh's resignation, citing a contradiction between his earlier statement and the official acknowledgement of deaths. While the Ministry of Defence has rejected the allegations, stating Singh's speech was selectively quoted, the Opposition plans to raise the issue during the upcoming Monsoon Session of Parliament.
Content:
The Congress has stepped up its attack on Defence Minister Rajnath Singh after the government officially disclosed the names of six Indian military personnel who were killed during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. The party has accused Singh of misleading Parliament by stating that no Indian soldiers were harmed during the operation and has demanded his resignation, arguing that the statement contradicted the government's subsequent acknowledgement of military casualties.

Congress MP KC Venugopal has submitted a privilege motion against the Defence Minister, while the Opposition is expected to raise the issue during the Monsoon Session of Parliament, scheduled to run from July 20 to August 13.

The controversy stems from the government's recent decision to publicly disclose the identities of six Indian military personnel who lost their lives during Operation Sindoor. Their names have been added to the Roll of Honour on the National War Memorial website and engraved at the National War Memorial in New Delhi, marking the first formal public acknowledgement of Indian armed forces casualties during the operation.

The six personnel named are Subedar Major Pawan Kumar, Rifleman Sunil Kumar (Vir Chakra), Lance Naik Dinesh Kumar, Aviation Technician Mood Muralinaik, Havildar Sunil Kumar Singh and Sergeant Surendra Kumar (Vayu Medal).

Congress argues that this official acknowledgement contradicts Rajnath Singh's statement in Parliament in July 2025 that no Indian soldiers were harmed during the operation.

At a press conference in New Delhi, Colonel Rohit Chaudhary, chairman of the Congress's ex-servicemen department, and retired Wing Commander Anuma Acharya accused the Defence Minister of making a false statement in Parliament on July 28, 2025.

The party described the remark as an insult to the country's fallen soldiers and demanded an apology from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Rajnath Singh and the BJP leadership to the families of the soldiers, the armed forces and the nation.

The party questioned why it took 13 months for the names of soldiers killed during Operation Sindoor to be officially disclosed. Chaudhary alleged that 10 soldiers had died during the operation, claiming that while six names had recently been added to the National War Memorial, four others remained unaccounted for.

The controversy centres on remarks made by Rajnath Singh during a Lok Sabha discussion on July 28, 2025.

Responding to questions on the operation, Singh said, "If you want to raise a question, then ask whether any of our brave soldiers were harmed in this operation. The answer is, no, none of our soldiers were harmed."

He also dismissed Opposition questions regarding military aircraft losses, saying such questions did "not adequately represent our national sentiments."

According to Singh, the focus should remain on the success of Operation Sindoor in destroying terrorist infrastructure, adding that the armed forces halted operations only after achieving all politico-military objectives.

Congress maintains that these remarks are inconsistent with the government's subsequent public acknowledgement of six military casualties.

The Ministry of Defence has rejected allegations that Rajnath Singh misled Parliament. According to the ministry, social media posts selectively quoted a portion of the Defence Minister's speech to create a misleading impression.

The ministry said these posts had "selectively quoted an isolated portion of the speech to falsely imply that the defence minister claimed that no Indian soldier lost his life during Operation Sindoor".

The clarification came after the issue gained political attention following the government's disclosure of the names of the six personnel honoured at the National War Memorial.

Congress MP KC Venugopal has submitted a privilege motion against Rajnath Singh under Rule 223 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.

In his notice to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, Venugopal argued that the Defence Minister's statement on the floor of the House was inconsistent with the government's later disclosure of casualties.

"The aforementioned position clearly indicates that the Minister of Defence stating on the floor of the House that there had been no casualties during Operation Sindoor was clearly misleading and incorrect. It is well established that misleading the House or withholding information by a Minister on the Floor of the House constitutes a breach of privilege and contempt of the House," Venugopal wrote.

He requested that "privilege proceedings may be initiated against the Minister of Defence in the matter."

A privilege motion is a parliamentary mechanism through which MPs can raise allegations that a member or minister has breached the privileges of the House, including by allegedly misleading Parliament. The Speaker decides whether such a notice merits further examination.

The Monsoon Session of Parliament is scheduled to be held from July 20 to August 13.

The Opposition is expected to press the government over Rajnath Singh's remarks and seek discussion on the privilege motion submitted by KC Venugopal. Congress is also likely to demand explanations over the delay in publicly disclosing the names of personnel killed during Operation Sindoor and question the government's handling of information related to the military operation.

Heading: CPI's Protest March Against Rajnath Singh's Statement, Demands Resignation
Summary: The Communist Party of India (CPI) organized a protest march in Samastipur, demanding the resignation of Defense Minister Rajnath Singh over his alleged statement regarding soldiers martyred during Operation Sindoor. CPI leaders accused the government of misleading the country. Additionally, speakers at the rally called for an impartial investigation into alleged irregularities concerning donations to the Ayodhya Ram Temple Trust.
Content:
Samastipur News: A protest march was organized in Samastipur under the banner of the District Council of the Communist Party of India (CPI). Protesters opposed the alleged statement of Defense Minister Rajnath Singh and demanded his resignation. Content:

 Delayed honour: On Operation Sindoor, gains and losses

The Union minister asserted that after Operation Sindoor, "trust in made-in-India defence platforms has got enhanced".

 Armed forces ready for ‘Operation Sindoor 2.0’ if need arises, says Army chief

In his address, he also spoke of India's journey in various sectors in the last 12 years, the advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and the importance of human sensitivity in the age of AI, including in the field of journalism.

The event was hosted in Delhi to mark 80 years of the national Hindi daily Navbharat Times.

"India’s journey over the last 12 years has been a progression from shortages to self-reliance, from self-reliance to self-confidence, and from self-confidence towards building a Viksit Bharat,” Mr. Singh said.

 India’s defence production hits record ₹1.78 lakh crore in FY 2025-26

Misinformation severely impacts society and the morale of defence forces, he said, adding that while being the first to report may be important in journalism, disseminating correct news is even more crucial.

Heading: Bill for PM, CM removal over 30-day jail, row over Rajnath's ‘lie’ may dominate Parliament monsoon session from July 20
Summary: The upcoming Monsoon Session of Parliament is expected to be dominated by a controversial bill proposing the automatic removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers, and ministers if held in judicial custody for 30 days, and a breach-of-privilege motion against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. The article outlines the significant constitutional hurdles for the bill, requiring special majorities and state ratification, and the political strategies involved in securing its passage. It also covers the opposition's accusations against Rajnath Singh regarding his statements on Operation Sindoor and the government's defense.
Content:
The BJP-led central government's controversial proposal to automatically remove the prime minister, chief ministers and ministers from office if they remain in judicial custody for30 consecutive days, along with a brewing row over defence minister Rajnath Singh's remarks on Operation Sindoor, is set to dominate the Monsoon Session of Parliament beginning July 20.

The government on Saturday announced that the sessionwill run until August 13.Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said President Droupadi Murmu had approved summoning both Houses from July 20 “for meaningful debate, discussion and decisions on issues of national importance”.

The spotlight is expected to fall on the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025, after a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) examining the legislation is scheduled to meet on July 17 to adopt its report, news agency ANI reported on Saturday.

TheJPCis unlikely to recommend dropping the bill's contentious provision, which mandates the automatic removal of the PM, CMs and Union or state ministers if they are arrested and remain in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days in cases involving serious offences.

The report, however, is expected to recommend safeguards to prevent misuse through politically motivated prosecutions or vendetta, ANI reported citing unnamed sources but did not report further details.

The proposed constitutional amendment has emerged as one of the government's most debated legislative initiatives since it was introduced last year.

Plus, PM Narendra Modi's government could not make constitutional amendments in the last session as it does not have the Parliamentary numbers for that. Defections have changed the math a bit since; more on that later. First, the 130th Amendment Bill.

Supporters argue the measure to allow for removal of leaders, based on mere jailing on allegations, would enhance accountability in public office. Critics, however, contend that it fundamentally alters the constitutional framework. Rather, there could be faster court decisions, they have argued.

Even if the JPC submits its report before Parliament reconvenes, the legislation faces a substantially higher threshold than an ordinary bill.

Because it seeks to amend the Constitution, the bill must be passed separately by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha by a “special majority” under Article 368 of the Constitution.

That requires support of a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two-thirds of members present and voting. Since the amendment directly affects constitutional provisions governing executive offices, it is also expected to require ratification by at least half of the state legislatures before it can receive presidential assent and come into force.

This arithmetic is central to the political debate surrounding the Bill.

The BJP has evidently been working to improve its effective strength in both Houses through electoral gains, defections and support from non-aligned regional parties.

It has been seeking to advance other constitutional measures too, including legislation linked to delimitation and the implementation of women's reservation. That's the proposed 131st amendment which failed the Parliament test in April, underlining that the BJP or NDA does not have the numbers for sweeping changes, yet.

The fate of the130th Amendment Bill— on removal provisions for PM, CMs and ministers — is therefore being viewed as an important test of the government's ability to build consensus for constitutional changes.

The Opposition is also expected to aggressively pursue breach-of-privilege proceedings against defence minister Rajnath Singh over his statements during Parliament's discussion on Operation Sindoor last year.

The Congress, buoyed by recent shows of unity in the INDIA bloc, has accused Rajnath Singh of misleading the Lok Sabha by stating that no Indian soldier was martyred duringOperation Sindoor. The Rahul Gandhi-led Opposition argued that the government's subsequent official acknowledgement of military casualties contradicts that assertion.

Congress general secretary KC Venugopal has moved a breach-of-privilege notice against the minister, alleging he made a "straightforward, clear-cut lie" before Parliament.

The BJP and the government have argued that Rajnath Singh's remarks are being quoted selectively and out of context. They have maintained that the veteran leader was referring to a specific phase of the operation and not denying that Indian military personnel lost their lives during the broader course of hostilities.

Whether the privilege notice is admitted will ultimately depend on the decision of the Lok Sabha Speaker, Om Birla, who is also to take some key decision on recent defections to the BJP-led NDA from Bengal's Trinamool Congress and Maharashtra's Shiv Sena (UBT).

The NDA's improved numbers have strengthened its hand particularly in the Rajya Sabha, though they do not guarantee passage of a constitutional amendment.

Political estimates after the latest Rajya Sabha elections, defections and resignations put the ruling alliance at around 151 members, with the possibility of rising to 154 after bypolls to seats vacated by rebel Trinamool Congress MPs. In the current House of 245, a constitutional amendment ordinarily requires the support of at least 163 members, assuming full attendance. That would still leave the NDA roughly nine votes short.

However, the required threshold can change depending on attendance. Under Article 368, a Constitution amendment must, as first step, secure the support of a majority of the total membership of each House. Plus, it must be approved by two-thirds of members present and voting.

This means abstentions by Opposition MPs could reduce the second requirement. For example, if only 225 members vote in the Rajya Sabha, the two-thirds mark falls to 150.

In the Lok Sabha, too, absences can reduce the two-thirds threshold. That remains the tougher hurdle, though.

The current effective Lok Sabha strength is 540 owing to three vacancies, and a Constitution amendment would require 360 votes if all members vote. With the NDA's effective support estimated at about 320 MPs after recent defections, the ruling alliance still falls about 40 votes short of the mark if there is full attendance.

However, the threshold falls if Opposition MPs abstain — for instance, to 334 if only 500 members vote, and 300 if 450 members vote.

That means the BJP-led alliance would require support from more regional parties, cross-voting, or substantial Opposition abstentions.

Content:
The Monsoon Session of Parliament will be held from July 20 to August 13, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced on Saturday.

In a post on X, Rijiju said President Droupadi Murmu had approved the government's recommendation to summon both Houses of Parliament for the session.

"The Session will commence on 20 July, 2026 and continue till 13 August, 2026 for meaningful debate, discussion and decisions on issues of national importance," he said.

The upcoming session is expected to witness key legislative business as well as political confrontations between the government and the Opposition.

One of the major pieces of legislation expected to return to Parliament is the Constitution amendment bill linked to implementing the 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies.

The proposed amendment seeks a uniform 50% increase in the strength of the Lok Sabha and state assemblies to operationalise the women's reservation law, According to Economic Times.

The Opposition is also expected to press the issue of privilege proceedings against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh over his remarks in Parliament regarding casualties during Operation Sindoor.

Congress MP K C Venugopal had submitted a privilege motion to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla under Rule 223 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.

The Congress has alleged that Singh misled Parliament by stating that no Indian soldiers were killed during Operation Sindoor, despite the government later publicly naming six military personnel who lost their lives in the conflict.

In his letter to the Speaker, Venugopal referred to Singh's statement made during a discussion on the Pahalgam terror attack and Operation Sindoor.

"On July 28, 2025, during the discussion on the terrorist attack in Pahalgam and Operation Sindoor, the Minister of Defence stated as follows," Venugopal said.

The Congress leader noted that the government subsequently inscribed the names of five Indian Army personnel and one Indian Air Force officer at the National War Memorial in Delhi, marking the first official public disclosure of those killed.

"The aforementioned position clearly indicates that the Minister of Defence stating on the floor of the House that there had been no casualties during Operation Sindoor was clearly misleading and incorrect. It is well established that misleading the House or withholding information by a Minister on the Floor of the House constitutes a breach of privilege and contempt of the House," Venugopal said.

The Ministry of Defence has rejected the Opposition's charge, saying Singh's remarks were taken out of context.

According to the ministry, social media posts had "selectively quoted an isolated portion of the speech to falsely imply that the defence minister claimed that no Indian soldier lost his life during Operation Sindoor".

During his Lok Sabha speech on July 28, 2025, Singh had said:

"If you want to raise a question, then ask whether any of our brave soldiers were harmed in this operation. The answer is, no, none of our soldiers were harmed," Singh said.

The defence minister also dismissed Opposition questions on military aircraft losses, arguing that such issues did "not adequately represent our national sentiments." He maintained that the focus should remain on the success of the operation, saying the armed forces halted military action only after achieving all politico-military objectives.

Operation Sindoor was launched by Indian armed forces on the night of May 6-7, 2025, targeting terror camps in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in response to the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack, which killed 26 people, mostly civilians. Hostilities ended on May 10, 2025, after India accepted Pakistan's request for a ceasefire. The government has maintained that the operation remains paused rather than concluded.

Summary: Ram Madhav dismisses recent speculation about a Track-2 dialogue with Pakistan as a disinformation campaign, stating India will not engage while Pakistan uses terrorism as a state instrument. Content:
Calling the Track-2 buzz a disinformation campaign, Ram Madhav said India had no reason to engage Pakistan while terror infrastructure remained active.
Amid speculation over a possible Track-2 dialogue between India and Pakistan after a recent conference in Colombo, Ram Madhav has dismissed the buzz as a disinformation campaign and said New Delhi has no reason to resume engagement with Islamabad while Pakistan continues to use terrorism as a state instrument.
Writing in an op-ed for The Indian Express, Madhav, a senior BJP leader and president of the India Foundation, said the recent buzz around a “fictitious" Track-2 channel between India and Pakistan appeared to be a case of Psyop, or psychological operations, aimed at creating suspicion and confusion. He said the claim was picked up by sections of mainstream and social media in India without verifying what the Colombo meeting actually was.
At the centre of the controversy was an annual South Asia conference hosted by a London-based think tank. Madhav said the event has been held for more than a decade and is attended by scholars, former diplomats, military and intelligence veterans, and occasionally politicians and serving officials from several countries.
According to him, the Colombo conference had participants from the US, the UK, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Afghanistan and India. That, he argued, made it a multilateral academic event, not a bilateral India-Pakistan Track-2 dialogue.
Madhav also cited Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri’s clarification that the conference was not part of Track-2 diplomacy. He said Track-2 diplomacy refers to a bilateral dialogue channel that has the tacit approval of governments, and does not involve representatives from several countries.
‘Pakistan Wanted Engagement, India Did Not Reciprocate’
Madhav said he addressed one session at the Colombo conference and left. While the Pakistani side appeared eager for a formal engagement with India, he said that sentiment was not reciprocated.
Explaining India’s position, Madhav pointed to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s earlier outreach to Pakistan. PM Modi had invited then Pakistan Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif to his oath-taking ceremony in 2014 and later made an unscheduled visit to Lahore in 2015.
However, Madhav said Pakistan responded to those gestures with the Uri and Pulwama terror attacks, after which the Modi government decided to shut down most forms of direct engagement with Islamabad.
He argued that Pakistan is frustrated by India’s refusal to engage, especially as New Delhi continues to deepen ties with major global powers while ignoring Islamabad’s overtures. Under PM Modi, he wrote, India no longer wants to be viewed through the old India-Pakistan hyphenation.
Pahalgam, Operation Sindoor And India’s ‘New Normal’
Madhav said the Pahalgam terror attack showed that Pakistan’s approach towards India had not changed. He said the attack reinforced New Delhi’s belief that Islamabad continues to rely on terrorism as an instrument of state policy.
After Pahalgam, India launched Operation Sindoor and targeted terror camps inside Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, eliminating at least 100 terrorists. Madhav said PM Modi’s message after the operation was clear: such responses would be the “new normal" in India’s dealing with Pakistan.
He also referred to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s statement at the UN General Assembly that he wanted to “win peace" with India, but argued that Pakistan’s conduct on the ground did not match its public messaging.
Madhav said there had been no major terror attack in India after Pahalgam, but credited that to India’s security and intelligence agencies rather than any change in Pakistan’s behaviour.
He alleged that Pakistan continues to shelter terror infrastructure, referring to Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Saifullah Kasuri and Jaish-e-Mohammad’s recruitment efforts. He also said Indian forces had foiled multiple infiltration attempts from across the border.
‘Talks And Terrorism Can’t Go Together’
Madhav said Pakistan is now trying to project itself as a champion of peace, including after its role in efforts around the US-Iran peace deal. But, he argued, India has seen Pakistan’s “true colours" and remains firm on its long-held position.
For New Delhi, he wrote, the message remains unchanged: talks and terrorism cannot go together. Madhav said that was India’s consistent stand at all forums, including in Colombo.

Heading: Three Forces Buying Weapons Worth 52 Thousand Crores
Summary: The Indian government, through the Defense Acquisition Council led by Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, has approved the purchase of weapons worth approximately 52,000 crores for its three forces. This modernization initiative aims to strengthen India's defense capabilities, particularly in light of neighboring threats from China and Pakistan. The acquisition includes advanced weapons, missiles, drones, and anti-drone platforms for the army, navy, and air force.
Content:
Indian three forces are buying weapons worth 52 thousand crores. Modernization initiative led by the Defense Minister.

New Delhi: On one side, China. On the other side, Pakistan. The central government is active in strengthening the three forces further, keeping an eye on the two neighbors. On Friday, the Defense Acquisition Council (DAC) led by Defense Minister Rajnath Singh approved the proposal to purchase weapons worth approximately 52 thousand crores. The list includes advanced weapons, missiles, drones, anti-drone platforms, and several other important military equipment. India has been emphasizing modernization in the defense sector since Operation Sindoor. It is believed that a large number of weapons have been approved for purchase with this objective. However, everyone's attention will be on Kamikaze drones. Ukraine has repeatedly troubled Russian forces with the help of these weapons. The DAC has given clearance to the army to purchase various equipment including air defense systems. Permission has been granted for the navy to purchase multi-influence ground mines as well as establish land-based testing facilities. On the other hand, it is known that the air force will be able to acquire various military systems including satellites.

Heading: Counter-UAV systems among Rs 52K-cr defence acquisitions
Summary: The Defence Ministry approved defence acquisitions worth Rs 52,000 crore, including counter-UAV systems for the Army and a pseudo satellite-based surveillance platform for the Indian Air Force. These procurements also include shipborne unmanned aerial systems for the Navy and jet-powered kamikaze drones, along with various missile systems. The acquisitions aim to enhance India's military capabilities, strengthening the Army's anti-drone and anti-tank capabilities, improving the Air Force's ISR and telecommunications, and boosting the Navy's situational awareness.
Content: Drawing lessons from Operation Sindoor and the military standoff with China, the Defence Ministry on Friday approved a counter-UAV system for the Army and a pseudo satellite-based surveillance platform for the Indian Air Force. A shipborne unmanned aerial system for the Navy and a new category of jet-powered kamikaze drones for the Army were also cleared by the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), the apex procurement body of the ministry. The DAC, chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, accorded Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) — the first stage of the acquisition process and an in-principle administrative approval — for proposals worth Rs 52,000 crore. For the Indian Air Force, approval was granted for the procurement of High-Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS), which will provide persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), telecommunications and remote-sensing capabilities. The HAPS platforms will feature fixed wings similar to aircraft and will be powered by solar energy and onboard batteries. They are essentially ultra-long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicles that operate in the stratosphere, typically at an altitude of 20 km. A pseudo-satellite flies high enough to perform many functions associated with a geostationary satellite, remaining over a designated geographical area for weeks or even months at a time, but at a fraction of the cost of launching a satellite into space. Unlike conventional satellites, which eventually burn up or become space debris, HAPS can return to base, land on a runway and be redeployed. For the Army, the DAC approved the procurement of the Akash Tarang anti-UAV system, an electronic warfare platform designed to neutralise incoming drones. The Ministry of Defence said the system would provide effective anti-drone protection to Army formations. Rather than relying solely on kinetic interception through guns or missiles, Akash Tarang employs radio-frequency jamming, spoofing and other electronic countermeasures to disrupt the command links and navigation signals of hostile drones. The DAC also approved the procurement of jet-powered kamikaze drones, along with man-portable anti-tank guided missile (MPATGM) systems, medium-range surface-to-air missile (MRSAM) systems and very short-range air defence systems (V-SHORADS). The MPATGM will strengthen infantry units’ ability to counter armoured and mechanised threats. The MRSAM system will provide medium-range air defence against a range of aerial threats, while the V-SHORADS will enhance the Army’s close-range air defence capability. For the Navy, the DAC approved the procurement of Naval Shipborne Unmanned Aerial Systems (NSUAS). Equipped with advanced sensors, these platforms are expected to significantly improve the Navy’s situational awareness and surveillance capabilities.

Heading: Same as Original
Summary: The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), led by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, has approved military purchases worth ₹52,000 crore to significantly enhance the capabilities of India's armed forces. These acquisitions include advanced systems like anti-UAV electronic warfare, man-portable anti-tank guided missiles, and medium-range surface-to-air missile systems for the Army, Navy, and Air Force. This strategic move aims to modernize the military, improving its defence mechanisms, situational awareness, and overall combat readiness against various threats.
Content:
The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), headed by defence minister Rajnath Singh, on Friday gave its go-ahead for purchasing weapons and systems worth₹52,000 crore to boost the armed forces’ capabilities. The capability boost approved by the council — India’s apex defence procurement body — covers procuring a raft of systems, from anti-unmanned aerial vehicle (anti-UAV) electronic warfare system ‘AKASH TARANG’, man-portable anti-tank guided missile (MPATGM) systems to medium range surface-to-air missile (MRSAM) weapon system, the defence ministry said.

The DAC also accorded its Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) for buying the very short range air defence system (V-SHORADS), an active protection system for tanks, and a jet-based kamikaze drone system, the ministry added in a statement.

The military hardware listed above is for the army.

Under India’s defence procurement rules, AoN by the council is the first step towards buying military equipment. It was for the first time the DAC convened after India’s new military leadership took charge under chief of defence staff General NS Raja Subramani, navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan and army chief General Dhiraj Seth. The top appointments were made recently.

Seth, who took over as army chief on June 30, said on Wednesday that the force’s modernisation would form the bedrock of its transformation into a future-ready force.

The defence ministry outlined the capability boost: AKASH TARANG will provide effective anti-UAV protection to army formations; the MPATGM will enhance the infantry’s potential to counter the adversary’s mechanised threats; and the MRSAM system provides medium range air defence against various stand-off aerial threats.

“The V-SHORADS with multi-spectral sensing will enhance counter-measure resilience and effectiveness of the Indian Army. The active protection system will improve the defence mechanism of tanks and enhance their survivability. The jet-based kamikaze drones will provide better electronic warfare capability with greater lethality and survivability while also being cost effective,” the ministry said.

The military hardware approved for the Navy includes the multi-influence ground mine (MIGM), the naval shipborne unmanned aerial system (NSUAS) and the establishment of a land-based testing facility (LBTF) for electric propulsion systems. “The MIGM will deny freedom of manoeuvre to the adversary. The NSUAS, equipped with advanced sensors, will enhance the Indian Navy’s situational awareness. The LBTF will meet the testing requirements for motors and associated propulsion systems of the Indian naval assets,” it said.

The Indian Air Force received approval to procure the fixed-wing based high altitude pseudo satellite (FW-HAPS). It will carry out intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), telecommunication and remote sensing for the air force, the ministry added.

In February, India hiked its defence spending by more than 15% against the backdrop of Operation Sindoor, setting aside₹7.85 lakh crore for the critical sector in the Union Budget for 2026-27. This included a capital outlay of₹2.19 lakh crore to boost the capabilities of the armed forces with new weapons and systems including fighter planes, transport aircraft, helicopters, warships, submarines, artillery guns, smart weapons, missiles, rockets and a variety of unmanned systems.

Heading: Is Peace Possible Between India and Pakistan?.. Diplomatic Challenges Amidst Terrorism and Security
Summary: The article argues against the feasibility of peace talks between India and Pakistan, despite calls from intellectuals, citing Pakistan's continued support for terrorism and its military's dominant role in foreign policy. It emphasizes India's firm stance on national security, its strategic actions like 'Operation Sindoor' and reviewing the Indus Waters Treaty, and the transformed geopolitical landscape of Kashmir post-Article 370 abrogation. The author concludes that genuine peace is unattainable until Pakistan addresses terrorism, respects agreements, and achieves internal stability, asserting that India's sovereignty and security cannot be compromised.
Content:
India-Pakistan relations have been an unresolved puzzle for decades, marked by uncertainty where danger can emerge from any side amidst sparks of tension. In such critical times, a joint letter from 117 intellectuals, diplomats, and political leaders from both countries to the Prime Ministers of India and Pakistan, advocating "We want peace... talks must happen," sounds theoretically appealing. Proposals like the restoration of diplomatic ties, appointment of High Commissioners, revival of trade borders, and expansion of cultural-religious corridors, while attractive from a humanitarian perspective, remain mere impractical ideals in the face of harsh ground realities and sharp geopolitical truths. At a time when the wounds of the Pahalgam terror attack are still fresh, and India has further tightened its military strategy through 'Operation Sindoor', there is no doubt that this peace mantra from intellectuals creates a kind of diplomatic illusion.

For a peaceful environment to emerge between the two countries, clarity on some fundamental and highly complex issues is essential. The first and most crucial is "ending systemic support for terrorism." Any peace talks will remain a mere farce until Pakistan completely suppresses cross-border terrorism originating from its territory. India has consistently maintained for decades that "terrorism and talks cannot go hand in hand." When incidents like the Pahalgam attack occur, engaging in diplomatic talks until the Pakistani military establishment ceases its financial and strategic patronage to terrorist organizations would mean jeopardizing our nation's security. Before peace talks, Pakistan needs to demonstrate its sincerity in dismantling terrorist networks through actions, not just words.

The second crucial aspect is mutual respect for past agreements between the two countries and clarity on changing strategic circumstances. India recently undertook extraordinary measures like reviewing and suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. This signifies India's readiness to act firmly in its national interest. Intellectuals, in their letter, called for revisiting the framework of talks held between 2004 and 2007 and for military de-escalation in Jammu and Kashmir. However, after the abrogation of Article 370 in 2019, Kashmir's geographical and political landscape has completely transformed. A fundamental question arises here: are Pakistan's rulers or its military prepared to accept this historical change and India's sovereignty? Coming to talks with a mindset unwilling to accept internal changes will yield no results.

Third is the flaw in Pakistan's internal balance of power. It is a well-known truth that the democratically elected government in Pakistan does not have full control over foreign and defense policies. Even if the political leadership in Islamabad is inclined towards talks with India, those discussions will not progress until the military headquarters in Rawalpindi gives the green light. Past events, such as the Kargil War immediately following Atal Bihari Vajpayee's Lahore bus journey, and the Pathankot attack just days after Narendra Modi met Nawaz Sharif, are living proofs of this. For the Pakistani army to maintain its existence, animosity with India must constantly simmer. Therefore, until the Pakistani army changes its strategic doctrine, any assurances given by the civilian government there hold no value.

The fourth aspect is changing international equations and China's role. Pakistan is currently entirely dependent on China's strategic support through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. China uses Pakistan as a pawn to contain India in the subcontinent. In such circumstances, India-Pakistan talks are no longer merely a bilateral issue; they have become a strategic chessboard for international powers. Pakistan currently lacks the economic and political stability to overcome the pressure of these international alliances and independently choose a path to peace. Pakistan, which is kneeling before the international community to overcome its own economic crisis, is not in a position to hold talks with India as an equal and reliable partner.

Finally, the internal political consensus and public opinion in India are also not favorable for peace talks. As BJP National Spokesperson Shehzad Poonawalla stated, ignoring the sacrifices of martyrs who laid down their lives protecting the country's borders and resuming talks with a country that harbors terrorism would mean encouraging a "terrorist sympathizer" attitude. Restoring diplomatic relations in a way that weakens India's strategic victory achieved through 'Operation Sindoor' and its strong defense policy is also not politically feasible. While it is good for intellectuals to talk about the welfare of two billion people, peace achieved by compromising national security and sovereignty can never be permanent.

In conclusion, words like peace, talks, and connectivity sound like a beautiful poem. However, amidst the constant threat of terrorism, a history of betrayal, and the nefarious strategies of the Pakistani military establishment, that poem turns into a bitter reality in practice. While one can understand the earnestness in the anguish of the 117 intellectuals, it must be said that under current geopolitical circumstances, peace talks between India and Pakistan are impossible. Until terrorist factories across the border are shut down, and respect for historical agreements grows, these peace letters will remain mere words in intellectuals' diaries, unable to become milestones in diplomatic history.
